 RBI rate hike puts household finances under pressure
 Policy Circle Bureau — 
 October 26, 2026 
 comments off 
 -->
 India's growing household debt raises concerns over the impact of RBI rate hikes on consumption, savings and loan repayments. 
 Written by   Policy Circle Bureau 
 RBI rate hike puts household finances under pressure: The Reserve Bank of India’s decision to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% in October has renewed concerns about the ability of Indian households to absorb higher borrowing costs. The increase is modest compared with previous tightening cycles, but families are already contending with expensive essentials, accumulated debt and uncertainty over income growth. Even a limited rise in equated monthly instalments (EMIs) could force households to reconsider their spending and saving decisions.
 The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised the policy rate on October 7 and shifted its stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. The minutes released on October 21 indicate that another increase or a pause are the likely options in the coming months, depending on inflation and growth. All six members supported the rate increase, although two preferred to retain the neutral stance. The disagreement over the stance reflects the difficulty of containing inflation without unnecessarily restricting economic activity.
 READ |  Retail inflation surge puts RBI’s growth priorities to test 
 Economists generally expect a relatively shallow tightening cycle, although the extent of further increases remains uncertain. This would be considerably less severe than the 250-basis-point increase between May 2022 and February 2023, when the repo rate rose from 4% to 6.5%. The impact on borrowers, however, will depend as much on their existing financial commitments as on the eventual policy rate.
 Why the RBI rate hike could hurt households
 During the pandemic, interest rates fell to historically low levels. The subsequent recovery released pent-up demand for travel, dining and other discretionary spending. Some households had also accumulated savings during the initial lockdowns, when opportunities to spend were restricted. The tightening that followed therefore began from an unusually accommodative monetary environment. The present cycle is unfolding against a different financial background, with households facing higher living costs and uncertainty about future earnings.
 A household pays its home loan EMI from the income remaining after meeting expenditure on food, transport, education and healthcare. When essential expenses rise faster than earnings, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can reduce the money available for other purposes.
 Consider a ₹40 lakh home loan with a remaining repayment period of 20 years and an interest rate of 8%. A 25-basis-point increase would raise the rate to 8.25%, assuming the lender passes on the full increase. If the borrower maintains the original tenure, the monthly EMI would rise from approximately ₹33,458 to ₹34,083. The additional ₹625 a month would add about ₹1.5 lakh to the total interest bill over the repayment period.
 If the EMI remains unchanged, the repayment period could instead extend by nearly 12 months, increasing the total interest burden by approximately ₹4 lakh. These calculations assume a constant interest rate after the increase and an unchanged outstanding principal. In practice, the effect will depend on the loan’s benchmark, reset provisions and remaining tenure.
 The immediate increase in the EMI may appear manageable, particularly for borrowers with steady incomes. But those who maintain their repayment schedule will have less money available for other expenses. Borrowers who extend their tenure will remain indebted longer and pay considerably more interest.
 Neither option is equally accessible to all borrowers. Older homeowners approaching retirement may have limited scope to extend their repayment periods, while families already servicing several loans may struggle to accommodate a higher EMI. Banks’ tenure restrictions and borrowers’ repayment capacity will determine how much flexibility is available.
 READ |  RBI bets on 7.1% GDP growth as inflation risks return 
 Rising household debt adds to the pressure
 Household indebtedness makes the current monetary tightening more consequential. The RBI’s December 2025 Financial Stability Report estimated household debt at 41.3% of GDP at the end of March 2025, against a five-year average of 38.3%. Non-housing retail loans, mostly taken for consumption, accounted for 55.3% of household borrowing from financial institutions in September 2025.
 The RBI’s June 2026 Financial Stability Report presents a more recent picture. Household debt had risen to 45.5% of GDP by September 2025, while non-housing retail loans accounted for 58.4% of household borrowings by March 2026. The increasing reliance on credit for consumption leaves some borrowers more exposed to changes in interest rates.
 There is an important qualification. Rising debt does not necessarily indicate deteriorating household finances. The RBI has found that the proportion of better-rated borrowers has increased, suggesting greater resilience across the household sector. Aggregate indicators, however, can conceal differences between households with substantial savings and those with little income left after servicing existing loans.
 READ |  US interest rates are testing RBI’s rupee stance 
 Higher borrowing costs could affect MSMEs
 The consequences of monetary tightening extend to businesses, particularly micro, small and medium enterprises that depend on bank credit for working capital. Higher lending rates can discourage investment and expansion, while businesses facing pressure on their operating margins may become more cautious about recruitment and wage increases.
 Such responses could reinforce the pressure on household finances. Families would face higher debt-servicing costs at the same time that some employers become less willing to raise wages or create jobs. The extent of this effect will depend on how much of the policy rate increase banks pass on to borrowers and how businesses respond.
 Inflation compounds the difficulty. Higher prices for essential goods reduce purchasing power immediately, while their effect on production and transport costs can eventually influence wages, employment and business profitability.
 The RBI’s inflation dilemma
 The MPC must balance these pressures against the risk of allowing inflation to become entrenched. Monetary tightening can restrain demand and prevent temporary price shocks from feeding into broader inflation expectations. A central bank that delays action for too long may eventually have to raise rates more sharply, imposing an even greater cost on borrowers.
 The difficulty is that India’s current inflationary pressures have a significant supply-side component. Volatility in international crude oil prices and the effects of a deficient monsoon cannot be directly corrected through higher domestic interest rates. The RBI can moderate the secondary effects of these shocks, but its principal instrument works partly by restricting demand.
 The October policy decision reflects this concern. The MPC raised its inflation forecast for 2026-27 to 5.2%, while projecting GDP growth of 7.1%. Its members recognised the risk of broader price pressures, although there were differences over the appropriate degree of monetary restraint.
 Further tightening may become necessary if inflation persists or spreads across the economy. Equally, the RBI will have to assess whether additional rate increases impose disproportionate costs on borrowers when much of the initial pressure comes from imported energy and agricultural supply disruptions.
 A smaller tightening cycle than the one witnessed in 2022-23 would limit the additional burden on borrowers. It would nevertheless leave intact the pressures from existing debt, expensive essentials and uncertain earnings. The RBI’s challenge is to contain inflation without weakening the very household spending and business activity on which economic growth depends.
